ARC Free Responses

ARC free responses

Three groups: Namibian participants with no schooling (n = 203), Namibian participants with some schooling (n = 117), and US participants (n = 68). One explanation per participant.

How explanations were coded

After choosing an answer, participants were asked why they chose it. Each analysed participant contributes one explanation (Namibian: English translation; US: verbatim transcript). Each explanation received one code. Coders go down the list and assign the first code that fits, so a stated reason outranks a guess.

CodeThe person…Example
Ruledescribes how an input becomes its output: something moves, falls, turns, grows, is added, removed, copied or recoloured, or a pattern carries over“the blocks fall to the bottom”
Resemblancejustifies the choice by sameness of colour, shape or form, without describing a change“they look alike”
Seeingrefers only to looking or pointing, with no feature named“I just saw it”
Guesssays they guessed, did not know, or could not work it out“I don’t know”
Preferencesays they liked it, wanted it, or that it is their opinion“It is beautiful”
Othernone of the above: remarks about the task or device, a bare feature (“it has more colours”), or unclear content“You didn’t explain to me well”

Procedure. The 388 explanations were shuffled and stripped of group, puzzle and accuracy. Two coders (independent Claude agents) applied the prompt below to every item. They agreed on 87% of items (Cohen’s κ = 0.83); on Rule versus any other code they agreed on 95% (κ = 0.89). A third coder resolved the 49 disagreements. The new codes match the earlier, undocumented codes on Rule versus not for 96% of explanations (κ = 0.91).

Limitations. US transcripts are fluent and longer, so coders could often tell them from translations. The scheme has no code for an explanation that names a feature without claiming sameness (“because it has less blocks”); these went to Other.

Exact prompt given to the coders 
You are coding short explanations from a visual puzzle task.

The task. Each puzzle shows a few example pairs: an input grid of coloured squares, an arrow, and the output grid it turns into. The same hidden rule turns every input into its output. The participant then sees a new input and picks which of four pictures is its output. Afterwards they were asked why they chose that picture. Some explanations are English translations of what was said in another language; others are verbatim English transcripts. Translations may be brief or ungrammatical. Code what the person says, not how well it is phrased.

Give each explanation exactly one code. Go down the list in order and assign the FIRST code that fits.

1. RULE
   The person describes how an input becomes its output: something moves, falls, turns, flips, grows, spreads, is added, removed, filled in, copied, recoloured, or counted, or a pattern carries over from one picture to the next. A vague description of a change still counts ("it turns that one into this", "the blocks go down", "the colour changes").
   Not RULE: saying only that the answer looks like or matches the examples.

2. RESEMBLANCE
   The person justifies the choice by sameness or similarity of appearance (same colour, same shape, same form, "looks alike", "matches") without describing a change.

3. SEEING
   The person refers only to looking or pointing, with no feature named ("I saw it", "this one", "that is how it looks to me", "it is the one").

4. GUESS
   The person says they guessed, did not know, or could not work it out.

5. PREFERENCE
   The person says they liked it, wanted it, found it beautiful, or that it is their opinion.

6. OTHER
   None of the above: comments about the instructions, the experimenter or the device; content that cannot be interpreted; empty.

Worked examples:
- "the blocks fall to the bottom" -> RULE
- "it is the same picture but the colour changed" -> RULE
- "I guessed but they are the same things" -> RESEMBLANCE (a reason is given, so it outranks GUESS)
- "I saw that they look alike" -> RESEMBLANCE
- "I just saw it" -> SEEING
- "I don't know" -> GUESS
- "It is beautiful" -> PREFERENCE
- "You didn't explain to me well" -> OTHER

Return one line per item as CSV with the header item,code and nothing else.

P1. Stating a transformation rule

P2. What people say instead

P3. Does stating a rule explain accuracy?

Test puzzles only. Each block shows the demonstration pairs and the test input as participants saw them, the picture the person chose, and the correct answer.

“Is the one that's on the bottom right”

Rule: Diagonal lines are drawn through each lone dot, across the whole grid.

“It is Beautiful”

Code: Preference

All explanations and codes

388 explanations, one per participant. Final code is the agreed code, or the third coder’s decision where the two coders disagreed. Namibian texts are English translations; most US texts are verbatim transcripts.
